16770:
Unseasonable means not fitting or suitable for the time.

That's the seed of the whole word. Everything else grows from it.

1. The Weather Sense (most common)

This is the sense you'll encounter most often in everyday life. When weather does not match what is normal or expected for a particular time of year, it is called unseasonable.

Every season has a "personality" — spring is mild, summer is hot, autumn is cool, winter is cold. When weather breaks this expected pattern in a surprising or dramatic way, it earns the label unseasonable.

Examples:

  • Heavy snow falling in late April is unseasonable, because snow belongs to winter, not spring.
  • A scorching 40°C heatwave in November is unseasonable, because such heat belongs to summer.
  • A freezing cold spell in July is unseasonable, because July is supposed to be warm.

Notice that unseasonable is not just about being unusual — it is specifically about being wrong for the time of year. A thunderstorm is unusual, but if it happens in monsoon season, it is perfectly seasonable. It only becomes unseasonable when it clashes with the expected character of that time.

2. The Timing Sense (less common, but important to know)

In this older and slightly more formal sense, unseasonable describes anything — not just weather — that happens at an inconvenient, inappropriate, or poorly timed moment.

Examples:

  • A loud phone call during a funeral is an unseasonable interruption.
  • Asking your boss for a pay rise while the company is losing money is unseasonable.
  • Arriving at a friend's house at 3 a.m. without warning is an unseasonable visit.

Here, the word is doing a slightly different job: it is judging the timing of an action as socially or practically wrong. You are doing the right thing at the wrong time.

This sense is less common in casual, modern English, but you will still find it in literature and formal writing.
The Crucial Difference: Unseasonable vs. Unusual

These two words can seem similar, but they are not the same.

  • Unusual simply means "not normal" or "not common."
  • Unseasonable specifically means "not normal for this particular time of year/moment."

A blue moon is unusual. But it has nothing to do with seasons. It would never be called unseasonable. In contrast, 35°C heat in December is unseasonable — because the wrongness is tied directly to when it is happening.

So unseasonable always carries a sense of mismatched timing. The thing itself might be perfectly fine in a different season or at a different moment — it is simply in the wrong place in time.

As a plain adjective (before a noun):

"The farmers were worried about the unseasonable frost."
"It was an unseasonable request."

As a predicate adjective (after a verb):

"The cold weather felt entirely unseasonable for June."

Its adverb form — unseasonably — is extremely common:

"It was unseasonably warm for January."
"He arrived unseasonably late."

In fact, you will often find unseasonably used even more frequently than the adjective itself, especially in weather reports and news writing.

• Seasonable (the opposite): fitting or appropriate for the time of year. "Seasonable rains helped the harvest."
  • Unseasonal: a synonym of unseasonable, used interchangeably in most contexts, though unseasonable is the older and more traditional form.
  • Untimely: a close cousin in the timing sense — meaning happening at a bad or unfortunate time. "His untimely death shocked everyone." (Untimely is stronger and often more final; unseasonable is milder and more about mismatch than tragedy.)
A Simple Test You Can Apply

Whenever you see or want to use the word unseasonable, ask yourself this one question:

"Is this wrong specifically because of when it is happening?"

If yes — it is unseasonable. If the wrongness has nothing to do with timing, then unseasonable is probably not the right word.

Unseasonable describes something — most often weather, but sometimes an action or event — that is inappropriate, unexpected, or out of place for the particular time of year or the particular moment in which it occurs.
16771:
To unseat someone means to remove them from a position they are currently holding — usually a position of power, authority, or dominance — and replace them, or at least push them out.

Think of it this way: someone is comfortably sitting in a position. To unseat them is to knock them off that seat. The "un-" prefix works like a reversal — it undoes the state of being seated in a role.

1. The Figurative Meaning (by far the most common)

This is how you will almost always encounter this word in real life.

To unseat someone means to defeat, overthrow, or remove a person from a role of power or leadership — often after a struggle, competition, or challenge.

The key idea is that the person being unseated had the position first, and now someone (or something) is taking it away from them.

"The young challenger unseated the reigning champion after a tough match."

"A newcomer unseated the long-serving senator in the election."

"The startup unseated the industry giant as the market leader."

Notice the pattern: in each case, there is someone established and powerful, and then there is a force (a person, a group, an event) that successfully removes them.

Important nuance: Unseating someone almost always involves effort, contest, or conflict. It is not a peaceful, voluntary handover. When a president simply finishes their term and steps down, we don't say they were "unseated." But if they are voted out, removed from office, or overthrown, that is unseating. The word carries a sense of displacement against resistance.

2. The Literal Meaning

Less common, but worth knowing. Literally, to unseat means to cause someone to fall off a seat — most often off a horse (or sometimes a bicycle or similar).

"The horse reared up and unseated its rider."

Here, "unseat" simply means the rider was physically thrown off or knocked out of the saddle. This is the original, concrete image from which the figurative meaning grew — the idea of being knocked off your seat.

You will mostly see this literal meaning in writing about horse riding, equestrian sports, or historical battle scenes.

"Unseat" is a transitive verb, which means it always needs an object — it always unseats someone or something. You cannot just say "they unseated." You must say who or what was unseated.

  • ✅ "She unseated the prime minister."
  • ❌ "She unseated." (incomplete — unseated whom?)

Common forms:

  • unseats → "He unseats the champion."
  • unseated → "She unseated the champion." / "The champion was unseated."
  • unseating → "They are unseating the current leadership."

It can be used in the active voice ("The challenger unseated the champion") or the passive voice ("The champion was unseated by a young challenger"). The passive voice is very common with this word, especially in news and politics.

The word is most naturally used with people or groups who hold formal positions of power or established dominance. Common examples:

  • Politicians — incumbents, presidents, senators, prime ministers
  • Champions and title holders — sports champions, defending winners
  • Business leaders — CEOs, dominant companies, market leaders
  • Monarchs or rulers — kings, dictators (in historical or dramatic contexts)
  • Institutional powers — a long-dominant ideology, a ruling party

It is less commonly used for everyday, informal situations. You would not typically say someone "unseated" a friend from their usual chair at the dinner table — unless you were being playfully dramatic.

"Unseat" is a neutral-to-dramatic word. It does not itself judge whether the removal is good or bad — it simply describes the act. Whether it sounds triumphant or unfortunate depends entirely on context and whose side you're on.

  • From the winner's perspective, unseating is a victory — a hard-fought achievement.
  • From the loser's perspective, being unseated is a defeat — a loss of something they held.

The word also carries a slightly formal register. You are more likely to read it in news articles, political commentary, sports reporting, or literature than to hear it in casual everyday conversation. However, it is not so formal that it sounds stiff — it is widely used across different types of writing and speech.

What it meansTo remove someone from a position of power, authority, or dominance — usually through contest, competition, or force
Who it applies toPeople or groups in established positions of power or leadership
Key qualityThe removal is earned through effort or conflict, not a simple, peaceful handover
Literal useTo physically throw someone off a seat, especially a horse
ToneNeutral to dramatic; slightly formal
One Final Way to Remember It

Picture a throne. Someone is sitting on it — confident, powerful, established. To unseat them is to pull that throne out from under them. It takes effort. There is usually a fight. And when it's done, someone else stands where that person once sat.

That image — the effort, the displacement, the shift of power — is the heart of the word "unseat."
16772:
Something is unseemly when it is inappropriate, improper, or unacceptable — specifically because it violates what society, a situation, or common decency considers right, dignified, or fitting. It describes behavior, actions, or appearances that look bad, feel wrong, or cause discomfort in others because they go against what is expected.

Think of it this way: every situation in life has an unwritten rulebook — how people should behave at a funeral, in a court of law, at a formal dinner, or during a serious conversation. When someone breaks those unwritten rules in a way that makes others cringe, feel embarrassed, or lose respect for them, that behavior is unseemly.
The Deeper Feel of the Word

"Unseemly" is not just about something being wrong in a legal sense — it's about something being visually and socially jarring. It's the feeling you get when something just doesn't look right to the people watching. There is almost always a sense of disapproval baked into the word.

It tends to suggest:

  • A lack of dignity or self-control
  • A disregard for the mood, gravity, or formality of a situation
  • Behavior that makes the person look bad in the eyes of others
What Makes It Different From Similar Words

This is important, because "unseemly" is easy to confuse with words like inappropriate, indecent, or improper.

  • Inappropriate is the most general of all — it simply means "not right for the situation." It's neutral and can apply to almost anything.
  • Indecent points strongly toward moral or sexual wrongdoing.
  • Improper suggests a violation of formal rules or etiquette — like using the wrong fork at a fancy dinner.
  • Unseemly is unique because it specifically carries the sense that something doesn't look right or doesn't fit in a social or moral sense. It carries a note of embarrassment or shame — not just rule-breaking, but looking bad while doing it. It often implies that other people are watching and judging.

"Unseemly" is a formal word. You won't hear it much in casual everyday conversation — people would more likely say "that was so inappropriate" or "that was so wrong." But you will see and hear "unseemly" in:

  • Formal writing (news articles, editorials, essays)
  • Literature and historical texts
  • Speeches or formal criticism
  • Situations where someone wants to sound measured and dignified in their disapproval

It also carries a slightly old-fashioned or traditional tone — the kind of word someone might use who has strong opinions about proper conduct and decorum.

One of the most important things to understand about "unseemly" is that it is deeply context-dependent. The same behavior can be completely fine in one setting and deeply unseemly in another.

For example:

  • Bursting into loud laughter is perfectly fine at a comedy show, but it would be unseemly at a memorial service.
  • Aggressively arguing for your own interests might be fine in a negotiation, but unseemly at a charitable event meant to promote goodwill.
  • Boasting about your wealth might be unseemly around people who are struggling financially.

The word always asks the question: given this specific situation, does this behavior fit? If the answer is no — and especially if it hurts dignity or makes people uncomfortable — it's unseemly.

Here are examples that show the word in action across different contexts:

Social behavior:
"It was unseemly for him to check his phone repeatedly during his colleague's retirement speech."

Emotions expressed at the wrong time:
"She felt that laughing at the accident scene was deeply unseemly."

Competition or greed:
"There was an unseemly scramble among the relatives to claim the inheritance before the funeral had even taken place."

Public figures:
"The senator's unseemly outburst in the chamber shocked even his own party members."

Workplace:
"Gossiping about a client during a meeting was considered unseemly behavior for a professional of her standing."

Appearance or dress:
"He showed up to the formal ceremony in shorts, which everyone agreed was unseemly."

"Unseemly" frequently appears with certain words. Knowing these patterns will help you recognize and use it naturally:

  • An unseemly haste / rush — doing something with an embarrassing, indecent speed (often used when someone rushes toward a personal gain at a bad time, like trying to profit quickly from a tragedy)
  • Unseemly behavior / conduct — acting in a way that lacks dignity
  • Unseemly dispute / squabble — a petty, embarrassing argument that makes all parties look bad
  • Unseemly spectacle — a scene that is embarrassing to witness
  • It would be unseemly to... — a polite but firm way of saying something should not be done

The direct opposite of "unseemly" is seemly — meaning proper, fitting, and appropriate. However, "seemly" is rarely used in modern English. In practice, people use words like appropriate, dignified, proper, or fitting to express the opposite idea.

You use "unseemly" when you want to express that something is socially or morally out of place — not just wrong, but visibly wrong in a way that reflects poorly on the person doing it. It's the word to reach for when you want to say: "This behavior doesn't belong here, and it makes everyone uncomfortable."

Ask yourself three questions before using it:

  1. Is there a clear social or moral standard being violated?
  2. Does it create discomfort, embarrassment, or a loss of dignity?
  3. Are other people (real or implied) witnessing and judging it?

If the answer to all three is yes, "unseemly" fits perfectly.
16773:
To unsettle something or someone means to disturb their calm, stability, or sense of order — pushing them from a state of being "settled" (peaceful, steady, composed) into a state of unease, uncertainty, or anxiety.

Think of it this way: imagine a glass of still water. When something drops into it, the water is no longer calm — it ripples and shifts. That is exactly what "unsettle" does, but to a person's mind, emotions, or to a situation. It shakes up what was previously at rest.

This verb is used in two main ways:

1. Unsettling a person (by far the most common use)

This means making someone feel mentally or emotionally uneasy — not quite comfortable, not quite at peace. The person starts to feel anxious, uncertain, or disturbed in some way.

  • "The doctor's vague answer unsettled him." — He was calm before, but now he feels uneasy and worried.
  • "Something about her smile unsettled me, though I couldn't explain why." — The person feels a quiet inner disturbance, a feeling that something is off.
  • "The horror film was expertly crafted to unsettle its audience." — It was designed to make viewers feel uncomfortable and uneasy.

2. Unsettling a situation or system

This means disrupting something that was previously stable, ordered, or functioning smoothly.

  • "The sudden resignation of the CEO unsettled the company." — The organisation, which was running normally, is now in a state of uncertainty and disruption.
  • "Political tensions unsettled the financial markets." — The markets, which were stable, became unpredictable and shaky.
The Feeling It Creates — and Its Intensity

This is important. "Unsettle" occupies a very specific emotional territory. It does not mean to completely destroy someone's composure, and it does not mean to mildly bore or annoy someone. It sits in the middle.

It creates a feeling that is:

  • Quiet but persistent — like an itch you can't scratch
  • Difficult to shake off
  • Not always explainable — you might feel unsettled without being able to immediately say why
  • Not paralyzing, but definitely noticeable

So if someone is terrified, that's stronger than being unsettled. If someone is merely surprised, that's lighter. Being unsettled is that uncomfortable in-between — a nagging sense that something is wrong, uncertain, or not right.
"Unsettle" always needs an object — something or someone must be unsettled. You cannot simply say "It unsettles." You must say "It unsettles me" or "It unsettled the situation."

Knowing these related forms will make the word truly yours:

Unsettling (adjective) — describes something that causes that uneasy, disturbing feeling.

  • "There was something unsettling about the silence in the house."
  • "The documentary raised unsettling questions about privacy."

Unsettled (adjective) — describes a person who feels uneasy, or a situation that is unstable or unresolved.

  • "She felt unsettled for days after hearing the news."
  • "The matter remains unsettled." (meaning unresolved, not yet decided)
  • "Unsettled weather" is also a very common phrase — it means unpredictable, changeable weather, not calm or stable.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Several words are close to "unsettle," but each has its own shade of meaning.

Disturb is broader. It can mean a physical interruption (like disturbing someone's sleep) or an emotional one. "Unsettle" is more specifically about inner emotional or mental instability.

Upset is stronger and usually involves clear sadness, anger, or distress. You know you are upset. Being unsettled is quieter and more ambiguous — you might not even fully understand what you're feeling.

Unnerve specifically attacks a person's confidence and nerve. It makes someone lose their boldness or composure under pressure. "Unsettle" is broader — it doesn't have to target confidence specifically.

Disconcert is very similar to unsettle, but it usually happens more suddenly — in a single moment — and often involves an element of confusion or surprise. You might feel disconcerted in an instant when something unexpected happens. Feeling unsettled can last much longer and build more gradually.

Perturb means almost exactly the same thing as unsettle, but it is more formal and used more in written or academic English.
The Subtlety That Makes This Word Special

What makes "unsettle" a rich and precise word is that it captures something that everyday language struggles with — the experience of being almost fine, but not quite. It is the feeling of something being slightly off, of a quiet alarm going off somewhere inside you that you can't fully explain or silence.

A truly terrifying thing does not merely unsettle you. But something deeply unsettling does not need to be terrifying to stay with you. A strange look from a stranger, an unexplained sound at night, a conversation that ended oddly — these things can unsettle you far more effectively than something obviously frightening, precisely because they leave your mind with no clear answer to latch on to.

This is why the word appears so often in literature, film, and psychology — it names a very human but hard-to-describe state perfectly.
16774:
Start with the word "settled." When something is settled, it is calm, stable, complete, and at rest — like a family that has finally settled into a new home and feels comfortable, or a long argument that has been settled and is now over. Unsettled is its exact opposite. It describes something (or someone) that has not yet reached that state of calm, stability, or completeness. Some form of disorder, discomfort, or incompleteness is still present.

This single core idea — the absence of being settled — branches into several specific meanings depending on context. Each meaning is distinct, but they all share that same thread.
Meaning 1: Feeling Anxious, Uneasy, or Disturbed (Emotions)

This is the most personal use of the word. When a person feels unsettled, they experience a quiet but uncomfortable sense of anxiety or unease — as if something is "off," but they can't always say exactly why. It isn't the sharp, intense feeling of being terrified or furious. It's more like a nagging discomfort that sits in the back of the mind and won't let you feel at peace.

"She felt unsettled after receiving the anonymous letter."
"There was something about his behaviour that left everyone feeling unsettled."
"He couldn't sleep — the day's events had left his mind unsettled."

A useful distinction: You say "I feel unsettled" when the uneasy feeling is inside you. You say "something is unsettling" when you're describing the thing that is causing that feeling. The adjective "unsettled" describes your inner emotional state; "unsettling" describes the external thing producing it. They come from the same root, and both are worth knowing.
Meaning 2: Not Yet Resolved or Decided (Situations, Disputes, Questions)

When a matter, question, debate, legal case, or dispute is described as unsettled, it means no final decision or conclusion has been reached yet. The issue is still open — it could go in multiple directions, and no one can say for certain how it will end.

"The question of who owns the land remains unsettled."
"There are several unsettled disputes between the two nations."
"Whether this drug is truly safe is still an unsettled issue in medical research."

You'll encounter this meaning often in legal writing, journalism, academic papers, and political discussions. It signals that something is genuinely unresolved — not just delayed, but truly without a clear answer yet.

This is one of the most common everyday uses of the word. When the weather is unsettled, it keeps changing in unpredictable ways — mixing sunshine, cloud cover, rain, and wind, often within the same day. It isn't necessarily a violent storm, but it isn't reliably calm or clear either. You simply can't count on it to stay the same.

"Unsettled weather is expected across the region for the rest of the week."
"We had a lovely morning, but the afternoon turned unsettled."

Weather forecasters use this word frequently. If you hear it in a forecast, pack an umbrella — but don't expect a full storm either. It's the weather equivalent of "unpredictable and unstable."
Meaning 4: Not Yet Paid (Finance and Business)

In financial contexts, an unsettled account, debt, invoice, or bill is one where the money has not yet been paid. The transaction is incomplete — one party still owes the other.

"Please ensure all unsettled invoices are cleared before the end of the month."
"The estate had several unsettled debts that needed to be addressed."

This meaning is straightforward but important, especially in business, banking, and legal writing.

"Unsettled" can also describe a part of the body — most commonly the stomach — that feels uncomfortable, uneasy, or mildly disturbed. An unsettled stomach is not in violent pain; it feels off-balance and not quite right, often without a clear cause.

"Rich food late at night always leaves me with an unsettled stomach."
"Anxiety can cause an unsettled feeling in your gut."
Meaning 6: Not Yet Inhabited or Established (Land and Territory)

When land or territory is described as unsettled, it means no permanent community has yet moved there, built homes, and established a way of life. The land exists in a raw state, without the structure and civilization that comes with human habitation.

"The explorers pushed further into unsettled territory."
"Much of the northern interior remained unsettled for centuries."

It helps to see the thread that runs through every meaning. Whether it's a person's emotions, an ongoing dispute, the weather, an unpaid bill, a queasy stomach, or uninhabited land — "unsettled" always points to the same idea: a final, stable, peaceful state has not yet been reached. Something is still incomplete, still in motion, still without resolution or rest.

"Unsettled" tends to sit in the mild-to-moderate range of intensity. It describes quiet disorder, not violent chaos. A person who is unsettled is not hysterical or broken — they are uneasy. A dispute that is unsettled is not a war — it is unresolved. Weather that is unsettled is not a hurricane — it is unpredictable. The word carries a sense of something being "not yet right" rather than something being catastrophically wrong.

Certain combinations with "unsettled" appear very frequently in English:

feel / seem / appear / remain / stay unsettled — used when describing a person's emotional state or an ongoing unresolved situation.

unsettled weather / conditions — the classic weather forecast use.

unsettled debt / account / invoice / bill — the financial use.

unsettled question / matter / issue / dispute / case — used when something has no clear conclusion yet.

unsettled stomach / feeling — used for physical discomfort.

unsettled land / territory / region — used for uninhabited areas.

Learning these patterns will help you recognize and use the word naturally across a wide range of real-world situations.
16775:
Imagine a giant boulder planted deep in the ground. You push it, kick it, and hit it with everything you have — but it does not move even a little. It stays exactly where it is, completely unmoved by your efforts.

Now take that same idea, but instead of applying it to a physical rock, apply it to a person's belief, faith, confidence, trust, loyalty, or determination. When any of these things cannot be weakened, disturbed, or destroyed — no matter how much pressure, doubt, hardship, or opposition is thrown at them — they are called unshakable.

That is the heart of the word.

Unshakable means: so firm, strong, and deeply rooted that nothing can weaken it, change it, or make it fall apart.

It describes a quality of the mind, heart, or character — not a physical object. When something is unshakable, it does not waver, crack, or collapse under any circumstances. It holds steady through everything.

The word is almost always used to describe inner, invisible things — things that live inside a person. Here are the most common ones:

Unshakable faith — a person believes in something (God, a cause, an idea) so deeply that no argument, tragedy, or doubt can ever pull them away from it.

Unshakable confidence — a person believes in themselves so solidly that failure, criticism, or mockery does not dent that belief at all.

Unshakable loyalty — a person's commitment to someone or something is so strong that betrayal, temptation, or hardship cannot break it.

Unshakable belief — a person holds a conviction so firmly that no evidence against it, no clever argument, and no amount of pressure changes their mind.

Unshakable resolve / determination — a person's decision to do something is so firm that obstacles, setbacks, and suffering cannot stop them.

Unshakable trust — a person trusts someone so completely that even rumors, doubts, or lies cannot disturb that trust.
The Hidden Meaning Inside the Word

Here is something important that makes "unshakable" richer than just "strong" or "firm."

When you call something unshakable, you are implying that it has been tested — or at least, that it could be tested — and it would survive. The word carries the idea of resistance to outside force. It is not just sitting there quietly; it is standing firm against something — against doubt, pressure, pain, challenge, or attack.

Think of it this way: a belief that has never been questioned is not really proven to be unshakable. But a belief that has been questioned, challenged, mocked, and attacked — and still did not move — that is unshakable.

So the word often paints a picture of strength under pressure. It suggests the quality has been (or would be) put to the test, and it passed.

"Unshakable" is a very strong, absolute word. It does not mean "hard to shake" or "difficult to change." It means impossible to shake — completely, totally, with no exceptions.

Because of this, it is not a word you use lightly. If you say someone has unshakable faith, you mean their faith is like that boulder — absolutely immovable, under any conditions, no matter what. You are making a very powerful statement.

This also means you do not add "very" before it. Saying "very unshakable" would be like saying "very unique" or "very perfect" — those words are already absolute, so adding "very" is unnecessary and incorrect. Something is either unshakable, or it is not.
How It Feels in a Sentence

Here are several examples across different situations so you can feel how the word works naturally:

"Despite losing everything in the flood, her unshakable faith kept her going."
→ Her faith could not be destroyed even by this devastating loss.

"He walked into the debate with unshakable confidence, knowing he had prepared for every possible question."
→ Nothing anyone said would make him doubt himself.

"The soldiers showed unshakable loyalty to their commander, even when others turned against him."
→ Their loyalty could not be bought, threatened, or broken.

"She had an unshakable belief that justice would eventually prevail."
→ No matter how long it took or how bad things looked, she never stopped believing.

"His unshakable resolve to finish the marathon pushed him through the pain of the final miles."
→ His determination was so firm that even physical suffering could not stop him.

Knowing the opposite of a word makes the meaning clearer and sharper. The opposite of unshakable is something that is easily disturbed, weakened, or changed. Words that capture this include:

Shaky — already weak, uncertain, and unstable.
Wavering — moving back and forth, not able to decide or hold firm.
Fragile — easily broken or damaged.
Doubtful / uncertain — not sure, not committed.
Weak — lacking the strength to hold steady.

So if someone has shaky confidence, a small failure can crush it. But if someone has unshakable confidence, a thousand failures will not touch it.
A Subtle Point: It Is Always Positive

When people use "unshakable" in everyday life, it almost always describes something admirable — a virtue, a strength, a quality we respect in a person. Faith, love, determination, loyalty — these are things we want to be unshakable.

You will rarely hear someone describe a bad quality as unshakable, though it is technically possible. For example, "unshakable arrogance" or "unshakable stubbornness" would use the same logic but describe a flaw. In these cases, the speaker is being critical — pointing out that someone's negative quality is so entrenched that even reason cannot change it.

But by default, unshakable is a word of admiration and strength.
If you had to remember just one thing: unshakable means so strong and firmly rooted inside a person that absolutely nothing — no pressure, no pain, no doubt, no force — can weaken or destroy it.
16776:
Imagine you are standing on solid ground. Someone tries to push you, argue with you, scare you, or give you terrible news — but you don't move. You don't waver. You don't doubt. You stay exactly where you were, mentally and emotionally.

That is what unshaken means.

"Unshaken" describes something — most often a feeling, a belief, a confidence, or a person — that has not been disturbed, weakened, or moved despite pressure, difficulty, or a strong reason to feel otherwise.
The Most Important Thing to Understand

"Unshaken" is not just a neutral word meaning "calm." It carries a very specific and powerful idea: something tried to shake it, and it failed.

This is the heart of the word. There is always an implied challenge in the background — a threat, a tragedy, a doubt, a piece of bad news, strong criticism, or a frightening situation. And despite all of that, the thing in question did not move an inch.

Without that implied challenge, the word wouldn't be needed. You wouldn't call a person "unshaken" while they're sitting peacefully on a sunny day with no problems. You call them unshaken after the storm — because the storm came, and they stood firm.
What Kind of Things Can Be "Unshaken"?

In everyday use, "unshaken" almost always describes abstract inner things — not physical objects. Here is what it commonly describes:

Faith or belief — When a person faces tragedy, loss, or doubt, but their faith or core beliefs do not weaken, their faith is unshaken.

"Even after losing her home in the fire, her faith in God remained unshaken."

Confidence — When someone is heavily criticized, mocked, or told they will fail, but their belief in themselves does not crack, their confidence is unshaken.

"Despite the harsh reviews, the young writer's confidence was unshaken."

Trust or loyalty — When a person goes through betrayal or difficult circumstances, but continues to fully trust someone or stay loyal, that trust or loyalty is unshaken.

"Years of hardship left their friendship unshaken."

Resolve or determination — When someone faces obstacles that would normally cause a person to give up, but they continue with the same firmness of purpose, their resolve is unshaken.

"The team's determination to win the championship was unshaken after their early losses."

A person themselves — Sometimes the whole person is described as unshaken, meaning their overall composure, calmness, or mental state was not disturbed.

"She delivered the difficult news and stood before the cameras, unshaken and composed."

"Unshaken" is a word that carries strength, dignity, and quiet power. It is almost always a compliment. When you describe someone or something as unshaken, you are suggesting that there is something admirable and solid about them — a kind of inner toughness that does not crack under pressure.

It is not a loud, boastful kind of strength. It is more like a rock that simply remains, no matter how many waves crash against it.

"Unshaken" is an absolute word. It does not mean "mostly fine" or "a little bit disturbed but recovering." It means completely unmoved. Not a tremor. Not a crack. Nothing changed.

This makes it a strong, committed word. When a writer or speaker chooses "unshaken," they are making a clear, firm statement — not a soft one.

Since learners often confuse words that feel similar, here is how "unshaken" differs from its close relatives:

Unshaken vs. Unmoved: "Unmoved" can simply mean someone felt no emotion — it can actually suggest coldness or indifference. "Unshaken" always suggests strength in the face of something difficult. It is warmer and more admirable.

Unshaken vs. Unwavering: "Unwavering" focuses on consistency over time — never going back and forth, always pointing in the same direction. "Unshaken" focuses specifically on the impact (or lack of impact) of a difficult moment or force. Both are very close, but "unshaken" always implies a test was faced.

Unshaken vs. Steadfast: "Steadfast" is about loyalty and commitment over a long period of time. "Unshaken" can be about a single moment or an ongoing state, and is specifically about resisting a disturbing force.

Unshaken vs. Unflinching: "Unflinching" is about not showing fear or hesitation, especially when facing something scary or painful. "Unshaken" is broader — it covers belief, confidence, trust, and emotion, not just fear.

"Unshaken" is a slightly formal and literary word. You are more likely to see it in a book, a speech, a news article, or thoughtful writing than in a casual conversation with a friend. In everyday speech, people might instead say things like "she didn't let it get to her" or "he held his ground" — but in writing or more formal contexts, "unshaken" is a precise and powerful choice.
A Final Picture to Lock It In

Think of a tall, old tree in the middle of a violent storm. The wind howls. The rain batters it. Everything around it bends and breaks. But the tree's roots go so deep that it stands perfectly firm when the storm passes.

That tree is unshaken.

Now replace the tree with a person's belief, confidence, faith, or spirit — and you have the word in its full human meaning.
16777: Unshod simply means not wearing shoes — or, for an animal like a horse, not fitted with horseshoes. That's it at the heart of it. But there's more texture to this word than that one-line definition suggests, so let's unpack it fully.

The word is built from two parts: "un-" (meaning not) and "shod" (the past participle of the verb "to shoe"). So if shod means "equipped with a shoe or shoes," then unshod means the exact opposite — without shoes of any kind.

When describing a person, unshod means barefoot — with no shoes, boots, sandals, slippers, or any kind of footwear on the feet at all. A child running across a grassy field with no shoes on is unshod. A monk walking barefoot on a dirt path is unshod.

"She walked unshod along the warm beach sand."
"The unshod pilgrims crossed the stone floor of the temple."
What It Means for Animals (Especially Horses)

This is where the word becomes particularly interesting, because unshod is very commonly used when talking about horses.

A horse that is shod has horseshoes — metal plates (usually iron or steel) — nailed or glued to the bottom of its hooves. This is done to protect the hooves from wearing down on hard terrain, to give the horse better grip, or for medical reasons.

A horse that is unshod has bare hooves, with no metal shoes attached.

"The unshod horse moved carefully over the rocky trail."
"Farmers debate whether horses should be kept unshod on soft pasture land."

This horse-specific usage is actually the word's most historically prominent application, which is why you'll encounter it frequently in literature, farming contexts, and historical writing about cavalry or travel.

Unshod is a formal, literary word. You won't hear it in everyday casual conversation — people don't usually say "I'm unshod right now." Instead, they'd just say "I'm barefoot."

You will, however, encounter unshod regularly in:

  • Literature and poetry (especially older texts)
  • Writing about horses, equestrian sport, or animal care
  • Historical or biblical writing (e.g., descriptions of wanderers, pilgrims, or soldiers)
  • Formal or descriptive prose where the writer wants a more elegant or dignified word

It's important to note what unshod does not refer to:

  • It doesn't mean poorly-dressed or sloppy in general — it is specifically about footwear (or the lack of it on hooves).
  • It doesn't imply poverty, neglect, or hardship by itself — it's a purely neutral, descriptive word. Context around it may suggest those things, but the word itself carries no such judgment.

IdeaWords
For peoplebarefoot, bare-footed, discalced (very formal/religious)
For horsesbare-hooved, unhorseshoed (though "unshod" is the standard term)
Opposite (with shoes)shod

(Note: "discalced" is a rare, very formal religious term — e.g., "discalced monks" — but unshod is more widely understood.)

Unshod = without shoes (for a person) or without horseshoes (for a horse). It is a dignified, formal adjective used most often in literary, equestrian, historical, or descriptive writing. It simply tells you that the feet — human or animal — are bare and uncovered by any kind of shoe or protective footwear.
16778:
Something unsightly is something that is unpleasant or offensive to look at — something that is ugly, visually messy, or disturbing to the eyes in a way that makes you wish you weren't looking at it.

Think of it this way: if something makes you think "ugh, that looks awful" or "I wish I couldn't see that", that thing is unsightly.
Breaking It Down Simply

The word is built from two parts: "un-" (meaning not) + "sightly" (meaning pleasant to look at). So unsightly literally means not pleasant to look at. However, it's stronger than just "not pretty." It carries a sense of being actively displeasing — something that stands out in a bad way and bothers people visually.
How Strong Is This Word?

"Unsightly" sits in the middle of the scale of visual unpleasantness. It is stronger than "unattractive" or "not pretty," but not as extreme as "hideous" or "grotesque." Here's a rough sense of the scale:

Not attractive → Unattractive → Unsightly → Ugly → Hideous → Grotesque

So when someone calls something unsightly, they mean it genuinely looks bad — not just slightly less beautiful, but visibly, noticeably unpleasant.
Is It Subjective or Objective?

Beauty is generally subjective, but "unsightly" is most often used for things that the majority of people would agree look bad — not things where opinions differ. You wouldn't call a painting "unsightly" just because you personally dislike its style. But a crumbling wall covered in mold, a pile of trash on a sidewalk, or a large grease stain on a carpet — most people would agree those are unsightly.

That said, the word can sometimes reflect a personal opinion, especially in context. If a neighbor calls your garden "unsightly," they're expressing their own judgment that it looks bad.
What Kinds of Things Are Called Unsightly?

"Unsightly" is most commonly used to describe:

Stains and marks — A large, dark stain on a white wall is unsightly.

Clutter and mess — A pile of broken furniture dumped on a lawn is unsightly.

Physical damage or decay — A rusted, dented old car abandoned by the road is unsightly.

Unwanted growths — A patch of weeds overtaking an otherwise neat garden is unsightly.

Blemishes on the skin — A large, inflamed rash or scar is sometimes called unsightly (though be careful — see the usage note below).

Urban or environmental eyesores — Graffiti on a clean building, wires hanging messily across a street, or a crumbling abandoned building in a neighborhood are all unsightly.

The common thread: something that should look normal or neat, but instead looks messy, damaged, out of place, or visually jarring.
The Tone and Register of This Word

"Unsightly" has a slightly formal or polished tone. It is more refined than just saying "ugly." You'll often find it in:

  • Newspaper articles and reports ("Residents complained about the unsightly construction debris.")
  • Formal complaints or official language ("The unsightly condition of the property violates community standards.")
  • Advertising for cleaning or cosmetic products ("Remove unsightly stains in seconds!")
  • Everyday speech, but when the speaker wants to sound a bit more composed or emphatic than just saying "ugly"
Examples in Sentences

1. The council voted to tear down the unsightly old factory that had been rotting at the edge of town for decades.
  2. She covered the unsightly crack in the wall with a large painting.
  3. After the storm, fallen branches and scattered litter left the park looking unsightly.
  4. The product claims to reduce unsightly dark circles under the eyes.
  5. He was embarrassed by the unsightly coffee stain on his shirt during the meeting.
  6. The tangle of electrical wires hanging above the street was considered unsightly by local residents.
  7. Overgrown weeds had made the once-beautiful garden completely unsightly.
Synonyms — and How They Differ

Ugly — The most direct and bluntest synonym. "Ugly" is stronger and more general. "Unsightly" is slightly more refined and often refers to visual messiness or disorder, while "ugly" can describe a wide range of things, including faces and abstract things.

Unattractive — Softer and milder than "unsightly." Something unattractive simply lacks appeal; something unsightly actively bothers the eye.

Hideous — Much stronger than "unsightly." Hideous implies something shockingly, almost offensively ugly. "Unsightly" is a moderate complaint; "hideous" is an extreme one.

Eyesore (noun, not adjective) — An eyesore is an unsightly thing. "That billboard is an eyesore" means the same as "that billboard is unsightly." Knowing this noun helps because you'll often see both words used in similar contexts.

Grotesque — Implies something disturbingly ugly, often in a twisted or unnatural way. Much more extreme and dramatic than "unsightly."
Antonyms — the Opposites

Attractive — Something pleasing to look at.
Beautiful / Lovely — Something that gives visual pleasure.
Pleasant — Something easy and agreeable to look at.
Neat / Tidy — In contexts where "unsightly" refers to mess or disorder, neat/tidy are good opposites.
One Important Usage Note

Be careful when applying "unsightly" to people's bodies or physical appearance. While it's grammatically correct, calling a person or part of their body "unsightly" can come across as very rude, harsh, or insensitive. The word is most naturally and safely applied to objects, places, conditions, and things — not to people directly. Interestingly, even cosmetic advertisements that use this word (e.g., "unsightly blemishes" or "unsightly scars") are technically describing a skin condition, not the person themselves — and that distinction matters in how the word lands emotionally.
The One-Line Summary
Unsightly means visually unpleasant in a noticeable way — something that genuinely bothers or offends the eyes, looking messy, ugly, or out of place, and making you wish it looked better.
16779:
Unsolicited means not asked for, not requested, and not invited.

When something is unsolicited, it means it arrived — or was given, said, or done — without anyone asking for it. The person who received it never made a request. It simply showed up on its own.

The word is built from two parts:

  • "Un-" is a prefix that means not.
  • "Solicited" comes from the verb solicit, which means to ask for something or to formally request something.

Put them together: un + solicited = not asked for.

That's really the whole heart of the word. If something was solicited, someone asked for it. If it was unsolicited, nobody asked for it — it came anyway.

This is where it gets interesting. "Unsolicited" is not always neutral. It often carries a mild negative undertone, because when something arrives that nobody asked for, it can feel like an intrusion, an imposition, or even disrespectful of a person's boundaries. It suggests that the giver decided, on their own, that the receiver needed something — without checking first.

However, unsolicited things are not always bad. Sometimes something unsolicited is a pleasant surprise. The word simply describes the nature of how something arrived (unrequested), not necessarily whether it was good or bad.

These examples cover many different situations where you'll encounter this word:

1. Unsolicited advice
Someone gives you advice about your life, your choices, or your work — but you never asked them for it. For example, you're eating lunch at work and a colleague says, "You really should eat less salt." You didn't ask. That's unsolicited advice. It's one of the most common uses of this word, and it usually feels unwelcome because it implies the other person thinks they know better than you about your own life.

2. Unsolicited email (also called "spam")
You receive an email from a company promoting their product, but you never signed up for their mailing list and never asked to hear from them. That email is unsolicited. In fact, in many countries, sending unsolicited commercial emails is actually illegal without proper consent.

3. Unsolicited feedback
A stranger reads something you wrote and starts telling you everything they would change about it — even though you shared it just to inform people, not to get feedback. Their comments are unsolicited.

4. Unsolicited help
Imagine you're struggling to carry your groceries to your car, and someone rushes over and grabs your bags without asking. Their help is unsolicited. (In this case, unsolicited doesn't mean bad — you might actually be grateful.)

5. Unsolicited opinion
You mention that you just bought a new car, and someone immediately says, "That's a bad choice, I wouldn't have bought that brand." You didn't ask for their opinion. It's unsolicited.

6. Unsolicited offer
A company sends you an offer to buy your house, even though your house was never on the market and you never indicated you wanted to sell. That's an unsolicited offer.
The Key Difference: Solicited vs. Unsolicited

SolicitedUnsolicited
Did the person ask?YesNo
Was it invited or requested?YesNo
ExampleYou ask a friend, "What do you think of my haircut?" — their answer is solicited.A stranger walks up and says, "Your haircut doesn't suit you." — that's unsolicited.

As mentioned, the word isn't always negative. Consider:

  • Unsolicited praise: Your manager walks by, sees your work, and compliments you warmly — even though you didn't ask them to review it. That feels good, even though it was unsolicited.
  • Unsolicited kindness: A neighbour shows up with a home-cooked meal when you're sick, without you asking. Completely unsolicited — and completely wonderful.

So the word describes the absence of a request, not necessarily the absence of value.
Why the Word Often Feels Negative (The Deeper Idea)

When someone gives you something unsolicited — advice, feedback, an opinion — there's an unspoken assumption they've made: that you need it. And making that assumption without asking can feel presumptuous or even rude, because it implies:

  • They didn't think your consent or preference mattered.
  • They assumed they know what's good for you better than you do.
  • They prioritised their own urge to speak or give over your right to decide whether you wanted it.

This is why the phrase "unsolicited advice" is often said with a hint of frustration, and why phrases like "nobody asked" have become common expressions of this same idea.
How to Use It in a Sentence

• "I didn't ask for your opinion — this is unsolicited feedback."
  • "She received an unsolicited job offer from a rival company."
  • "Please do not send unsolicited messages to other users of this platform."
  • "His unsolicited help was actually appreciated in the end."
  • "The email was flagged as unsolicited and sent directly to spam."

Unsolicited = something nobody asked for, but it came anyway.

Keep that in your head, and you'll always use and understand this word correctly.
